say: Drop a penny from the top of the Empire State Building and it could kill someone below. Everyone's heard it. So, is it true?
The building is one thousand two hundred fifty feet tall to its highest floor. That's a very long way down for one tiny coin.
With no air at all, a penny falling that far would hit the ground at around two hundred miles per hour. Okay, that does sound scary.
But a penny weighs just two and a half grams, and it's flat, like a tiny frisbee. The air pushes back on it, hard.
So it doesn't drop like a rock. It tumbles and flutters, like a leaf. After about fifty feet, it stops speeding up completely.
That top speed is called terminal velocity. Physicist Louis Bloomfield found a penny tops out around twenty five miles per hour. Other estimates say fifty, max.
If one hits you, Bloomfield says it feels like a flick on the forehead. Not even a hard one. Myth busted.
And at the Empire State Building, the wind rushing up the walls can be so strong, your penny might never reach the street at all.
The real danger? A ballpoint pen. If it falls point first like an arrow, it could hit at two hundred miles per hour. So please, drop nothing.
